ami_style_notes:
The meeting has mostly short-to-medium conversational turns, with a long, formal presentation style during talks and brisk, informal exchanges before and after them. Overlap and interruption are common but generally friendly: speakers jump in with quick acknowledgments, follow-up questions, or clarifications rather than adversarial challenges. The tone is collegial and lightly humorous, using frequent fillers and repairs such as “um,” “yeah,” “okay,” repeated words, false starts, and self-corrections. Participants hedge heavily in scientific discussion with phrases like “I think,” “sort of,” “maybe,” “it seems,” and “we’re interested in,” framing claims as provisional. Questions are often prefaced with praise or disclaimers—“great talk,” “naive question,” “I’m curious”—and tend to be multipart, exploratory, and conversational rather than tightly scripted. Disagreement is indirect and framed as uncertainty, alternative interpretations, or open questions. Speakers build on one another by referencing prior comments, restating a point before extending it, and offering collaborative suggestions or future follow-up.

Meeting style for this meeting (round_robin_updates): Each person takes a turn reporting what they have done since last time. Updates are fairly long and mostly uninterrupted. There are a few clarifying questions between updates and little cross-talk. The discussion that does happen is brief.
Illustration of the feel only (invented, do not reuse the wording or topic):
  - Okay, mine. I got through most of the interviews, I think fourteen of twenty, and the rest are scheduled for the following two weeks.
  - Fourteen, nice. Were those all from the first batch?
  - Most of them. A couple were referrals.
Opening: Start mid-thought, as if the conversation was already under way before the recording started.
Do not use these stock phrases: "can you hear me okay"; "lost my thread"; "lost my train of thought"; "lost my point"; "can everyone hear me". The recording does not need to begin with audio or login checks.
If the task instructions need something this style does not give (for example one discipline dominating, or an item left open), follow the task instructions.
research_problem: Working out why wild bee numbers on farms did not recover after wildflower strips were planted along field edges.

speakers.name: Dr. Asha Patel
speakers.background: Landscape ecologist with 11 years of experience studying pollinator responses to agri-environment interventions in mixed arable landscapes. She coordinates the 12-farm study, has assembled GIS layers for semi-natural habitat, hedgerow continuity, field-margin configuration, and likely movement corridors, and has led repeated standardized bee-survey protocols. Her field teams routinely quantify habitat structure, but nesting substrates and cavities have not yet been assessed consistently across the farms.
speakers.distinct_perspective: Frames the lack of recovery as a colonization and population-connectivity problem rather than evidence that the strips themselves failed. She is most persuaded by mechanisms operating across spatial scales: whether source populations can reach the strips, whether landscape permeability differs among farms, and whether nearby nesting opportunities allow foraging use to translate into local persistence. She favors a repeated, farm-wide design that integrates existing connectivity maps with systematic nesting-resource measurements and bee surveys, while treating species and farm-management information as explanatory context rather than competing causal claims unless they can be measured at adequate scale.
speakers.language_complexity: high jargon — uses discipline-specific terminology freely

speakers.name: Dr. Luis Romero
speakers.background: Pollinator biologist in the final year of his PhD, with six years of field and laboratory experience in wild-bee taxonomy, pollen-resource use, trait-based ecology, and pesticide biomonitoring. He can oversee species-level identifications from survey specimens, estimate plausible foraging ranges from species traits and published movement data, and coordinate residue or sublethal-exposure assays through an external laboratory. He has worked mostly on targeted studies rather than multi-farm intervention evaluations and is attentive to the logistical limits of specimen processing and laboratory budgets.
speakers.distinct_perspective: Sees abundance totals as potentially masking biologically important species-specific responses. He asks whether the flowers supplied by the strips are available when local species need them, whether strip plants match the diets and movement capacities of the bees present, and whether low-level pesticide exposure could reduce survival, navigation, or willingness to use the strips. He can support the follow-up with species identification and interpretation of foraging-range patterns, but is cautious about claiming that a mechanism is testable when exposure assays or floral-resource measurements cannot be funded at sufficient coverage.
speakers.language_complexity: moderate — balances jargon with accessible language
speakers.epistemic_stance: uncertain about how their methods apply to this problem

speakers.name: Dr. Mei Chen
speakers.background: Agricultural economist with 14 years of experience evaluating conservation-payment programs, farm adoption decisions, and yield-risk trade-offs. She maintains records on strip establishment and upkeep costs, subsidy participation, and crop-yield outcomes for the participating farms, and has conducted interviews and budget analyses with growers implementing field-margin schemes. Her current dataset documents broad management and financial conditions but does not include the detailed, repeated implementation audits needed to identify a causal management pathway across only 12 farms.
speakers.distinct_perspective: Treats ecological outcomes as inseparable from the incentives and operational constraints that shape implementation quality over time. She focuses on heterogeneity in maintenance, opportunity costs, subsidy design, and perceived yield risks, because a strip that is nominally planted may differ substantially in realized condition and farmer commitment. At the same time, she distinguishes management relevance from causal identification: existing cost, subsidy, and yield records can contextualize farm differences and improve the practical usefulness of results, but they cannot by themselves establish why bee responses differed without a larger sample and more granular implementation data.
speakers.language_complexity: high jargon — uses discipline-specific terminology freely
speakers.epistemic_stance: highly confident in their discipline's contribution

seed_spec.explicit_instruction: Run a planning meeting with Dr. Patel, Dr. Romero, and Dr. Chen. The team must consider four candidate research questions: (1) whether lack of landscape connectivity and nearby nesting resources prevented colonization of the strips; (2) whether pesticide exposure caused sublethal effects that limited bee survival or use of the strips; (3) whether the strips' floral composition and timing were mismatched to the foraging ranges and seasonal needs of the bee species present; and (4) whether establishment, upkeep, subsidy incentives, and crop-yield trade-offs led to management differences that reduced strip quality. Dr. Patel explains that a two-year, repeated survey design can pair bee surveys with nesting-resource measurements and existing connectivity maps on all 12 farms. Dr. Romero supports the pesticide and species/foraging questions but states that residue testing across farms would require additional laboratory funding not available for the current follow-up, while species identification can be retained as a supporting measurement. Dr. Chen says the economic records can be used descriptively but cannot establish the causal management pathway without a larger sample and detailed implementation audits. The group must choose candidate question 1 as the single primary question, with a 2026-2027 design comparing connectivity and nesting resources while repeating bee surveys. The meeting must explicitly leave questions 2, 3, and 4 unresolved rather than rejecting them, and must identify species-level identification and farm cost/yield records as supporting contextual data, not separate primary questions. Do not present any of the unresolved questions as answered.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Asha Patel
transcript.text: …before we get into it, I hope spring planning isn't already becoming impossible for everyone. What I'd like us to leave with today is a defensible primary question for 2026–27 across the 12 farms, and a clear sense of what we retain as context instead of trying to answer everything at once. Maybe we can- let's do quick updates first on what each of us has learned since we last met, and then narrow the design.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Mei Chen
transcript.text: …on the management side, I’ve pulled together the establishment and upkeep expenditures, subsidy participation, and crop-yield records for all twelve farms. The striking thing is, higher reported upkeep spending doesn’t line up consistently with either better or worse bee response. So I’d treat those variables as context, not evidence of a causal implementation pathway, unless we have detailed, repeated implementation audits. I still need to verify that the cost and yield windows line up exactly with the ecological survey farm-years…

transcript.speaker: Dr. Asha Patel
transcript.text: Mm, that alignment matters.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Luis Romero
transcript.text: …and on the specimen side, I’ve been rechecking the seasonal breakdown, not just the totals. Several farms barely changed in early-season captures, but the later surveys are much more variable. That could be flowering timing, a change in which species are present, or just weather, so I wouldn’t read too much into it yet. I need to check how many specimens we can take confidently to species across all repeated surveys without making the IDs— the identifications uneven.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Asha Patel
transcript.text: That seasonal asymmetry is useful, Luis. Before we decide whether species resolution is worth making central, what kinds of taxa are driving the late-season variation, and are they ones where our mapped corridors and semi-natural habitat ought to matter differently, given their likely foraging ranges? I’m also wondering whether the two apparently similar habitat-rich farms with very different counts are a warning that connectivity alone, or I should say without nesting-resource measurements, will be too coarse.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Mei Chen
transcript.text: Hm, that is a concern.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Luis Romero
transcript.text: The late variation does look like it includes a mix of smaller-bodied solitary bees and some broader-ranging taxa, but I’m not comfortable assigning that from the current IDs alone. And Asha, I was thinking about the corridor maps for the short-range species. How confidently do they represent actual movement, rather than just general landscape structure?

transcript.speaker: Dr. Asha Patel
transcript.text: They are proxies for structural permeability, not direct movement observations, particularly for the short-range solitary taxa. So I would not claim a corridor effect species by species from those maps alone. I think the defensible question is whether farm-level colonization and persistence after strip establishment are associated with landscape connectivity, conditional on local nesting resources. And the contrast between those two habitat-rich farms is exactly why we need that local, local measurement layer.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Luis Romero
transcript.text: I think species-level IDs are still worth retaining, but probably as interpretation around that question rather than the primary outcome. If nesting and connectivity explain the farm contrast, we can at least ask whether short-range taxa look different, but we shouldn't pretend the maps tell us where they actually moved. And pesticide exposure stays on the list. Meaningful coverage would need additional laboratory funding.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Asha Patel
transcript.text: I'd retain the species composition and seasonal pattern as effect-modification evidence, rather than spend the core design trying to resolve every taxon equally. The practical question for me is whether our field-team capacity can support repeated nesting-substrate assessments, bare ground, cavities, tussock structure, at all 12 farms in both 2026 and 2027. Without that, we can't really test the conditional part of the connectivity question.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Mei Chen
transcript.text: The repeated local assessments seem essential. Asha, would that protocol distinguish nesting resources actually within the strip from those in adjacent farm features? For the grower-facing interpretation, that distinction matters a lot. Otherwise, we may end up recommending strip investment when the operative resource is, say, unmanaged boundary structure outside it.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Luis Romero
transcript.text: Yeah, that distinction is important.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Asha Patel
transcript.text: I’d stratify the protocol explicitly. So we’d look at resource availability within the strip, at the strip–field interface, and in adjacent boundary features, instead of collapsing those into a single farm score. Across all 12 farms from spring 2026 through 2027, that lets us ask whether strips function differently where nearby nesting infrastructure is present, which is a lot more actionable than attributing everything to the strip itself, but...

transcript.speaker: Dr. Mei Chen
transcript.text: …good, that makes the interpretation much cleaner. I'd want to keep the management records alongside those strata descriptively, especially yields and subsidy terms, because a recommendation to preserve adjacent boundary habitat has very, very different feasibility depending on the opportunity cost to the grower. But I wouldn't try to infer from our existing records that maintenance caused the nesting pattern. We simply don't have the repeated implementation audits for that.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Asha Patel
transcript.text: …yes, exactly, that's the right boundary on what Mei's data can support. I'll check field-team capacity this week, but if we can sustain the repeated stratified nesting assessments, I think the primary question can be framed around whether landscape connectivity predicts bee recovery conditional on nesting resources within and adjacent to strips, with management feasibility kept alongside it.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Mei Chen
transcript.text: …and I think that framing gives growers something they can actually use, as long as we're careful not to turn the descriptive budget data into a mechanism. Once I confirm the farm-year alignment, we can show the yield and subsidy context alongside the nesting strata, whether protecting those adjacent features is feasible under the particular margins these farms…

transcript.speaker: Dr. Luis Romero
transcript.text: That seems like the most defensible focus, as long as we keep the seasonal species records alongside it.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Mei Chen
transcript.text: Okay, useful distinction.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Asha Patel
transcript.text: …then I think we have the shape of it. I’ll confirm whether the teams can repeat those three nesting-resource strata through both seasons. If they can’t- if they cannot, we should not overstate the conditional test. Luis, it would also help to retain the seasonal species records in a form we can relate to those strata and the connectivity gradient, even if the species analysis remains secondary.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Luis Romero
transcript.text: …yes, I can keep the seasonal records linked to the strip, interface, and boundary strata, assuming the specimen volume is manageable. I’d like to check the identification workload before I promise full species resolution at every visit. If it gets tight, even genus-level patterns for the smaller solitary bees may be more consistent. And if that late-season pattern persists, it might tell us whether the nesting contrast is interacting with floral timing, rather than it just being a simple connectivity story, but…

transcript.speaker: Dr. Asha Patel
transcript.text: Mm, yes—floral timing is a plausible modifier, not a competing primary mechanism.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Mei Chen
transcript.text: …I think we can give people a few minutes back. Thanks, both. I’ll check the farm-year alignment on my side, and we can pick this up once Asha has heard about field capacity.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Luis Romero
transcript.text: Okay, sounds good. Bye, both.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Asha Patel
transcript.text: All right, speak soon.
